_note: Research tier. Landmark studies with where they were coordinated. Every row cites its source. Coordinates are the lead institution, not where experiences happened.

studies.name: Dutch prospective study
studies.place: Netherlands (10 hospitals; lead author at Rijnstate Hospital, Arnhem)
studies.finding: 344 consecutive survivors of 509 successful resuscitations across ten Dutch hospitals, interviewed within days. 62 (18%) had some recollection of the time of clinical death; 41 (12%) a core experience and 23 (7%) a deep or very deep one. The 18% is the figure usually quoted. The authors concede possible selection bias: the one hospital that ran nearly four years and contributed 137 patients found only 8%.
studies.cite: van Lommel P, van Wees R, Meyers V, Elfferich I. Near-death experience in survivors of cardiac arrest: a prospective study in the Netherlands. The Lancet 2001;358:2039-45.

studies.name: AWARE
studies.place: Stony Brook, NY, USA (15 hospitals in UK, US, Austria)
studies.finding: 2,060 cardiac arrests across 15 hospitals; 330 survived to discharge, 140 were interviewed and 101 completed the second-stage interview. 9% of those 101 met criteria for an NDE and 2% described explicit awareness with recall of events. The published record is not consistent about these counts, so no raw numbers are asserted here.
studies.cite: Parnia S et al. AWARE: AWAreness during REsuscitation, a prospective study. Resuscitation 2014;85:1799-1805.
studies.no_walk: This study counted how many people had an experience, not what was in it. Its sister study AWARE II describes the content.

studies.name: AWARE II
studies.place: New York, USA (25 hospitals in US and UK)
studies.finding: 567 patients; EEG recorded during CPR in a pilot sub-study of some patients; 28 survivors interviewed; 126 community accounts analysed for themes.
studies.cite: Parnia S et al. AWAreness during REsuscitation II: a multi-center study of consciousness and awareness in cardiac arrest. Resuscitation 2023;191:109903.
studies.scene_note: AWARE II describes what survivors recalled as a separation from the body, observing events without pain or distress, travelling to a destination, and a meaningful evaluation of their own actions and relationships. The paper reports themes rather than percentages, so each stage plays at the same strength.

studies.name: Cardiac care unit study
studies.finding: 1,595 consecutive cardiac inpatients. 116 (7%) were admitted with cardiac arrest, and 11 of those (10%) reported an NDE, against 1% of the other cardiac patients. Across the whole cohort the rate was 27 of 1,595, or 1.7%.
studies.cite: Greyson B. Incidence and correlates of near-death experiences in a cardiac care unit. General Hospital Psychiatry 2003;25:269-76.
studies.no_walk: A prevalence study: it measured how often an NDE happens in a cardiac unit, not what the experiences contained.

studies.name: Southampton study
studies.finding: 63 cardiac-arrest survivors at Southampton General Hospital. 56 (88.8%) had no recall; 7 (11.1%) had some memory of the period, and of those 4 (6.3%) scored 7 or more on the Greyson scale. Two of the three below the threshold still had NDE-like features.
studies.cite: Parnia S, Waller DG, Yeates R, Fenwick P. A qualitative and quantitative study of the incidence, features and aetiology of near death experiences in cardiac arrest survivors. Resuscitation 2001;48:149-56.
studies.no_walk: A prevalence study in one hospital; the sample of experiencers was too small to publish feature rates.

studies.name: Childhood NDEs
studies.finding: 40 children aged 3 to 16 in a paediatric intensive care unit: 11 critically ill (7 cardiac-arrest survivors and 4 with a Glasgow coma score under 5) and 29 seriously ill age-matched controls. 7 of the 11 reported near-death elements. No control reported an NDE, though four recalled something, three of them intraoperative.
studies.cite: Morse M, Conner D, Tyler D. Near-death experiences in a pediatric population: a preliminary report. American Journal of Diseases of Children 1986;140:1110-14.
studies.no_walk: A comparison of critically ill children with a control group, reporting that NDE features occurred in one and not the other, without published rates per feature.

studies.name: Gallup poll
studies.finding: About 5% of US adults, then roughly 8 million people, reported a near-death experience.
studies.cite: Gallup G, Proctor W. Adventures in Immortality. McGraw-Hill, 1982.
studies.no_walk: A national poll of how many adults had ever had one. This atlas does not have verified figures for the individual elements it asked about.
studies.nature: About 1,500 adults were asked, between early 1980 and September 1981; Gallup's book does not give an exact sample size.

studies.name: German survey
studies.finding: 2,044 Germans in a nationally representative sample: 82 (4%) reported an NDE. Content split sharply east and west: 60% of west German accounts were positive against 40% in the east, where 60% were negative; tunnels were commoner in the east, light in the west. The rate itself did not differ. The authors ran no significance tests on these splits and call them 'only tendencies'.
studies.cite: Knoblauch H, Schmied I, Schnettler B. Different kinds of near-death experience: a report on a survey of near-death experiences in Germany. Journal of Near-Death Studies 2001;20:15-29.
studies.no_walk: A population survey measuring how many Germans had had one, and differences between East and West, rather than rates per feature.

studies.name: Australian survey
studies.finding: 673 Australians in a national telephone survey. 241 (36%) had come close to death, and 60 of them met the study's NDE criterion: 8.9% of everyone asked, or about a quarter of those who had come close. The 8.9% is computed from the paper's own table, which the text and abstract report variously as 9% and 8%.
studies.cite: Perera M, Padmasekara G, Belanti J. Prevalence of near-death experiences in Australia. Journal of Near-Death Studies 2005;24:109-16.
studies.no_walk: A telephone survey measuring how many Australians had had one.
studies.nature: The criterion was endorsing any two items from a telephone-adapted list, not a Greyson score of 7, and the authors note the prompts raised endorsement. This rate is not comparable with the hospital figures.

studies.name: NDERF survey
studies.finding: 613 experiencers scoring 7 or more on the Greyson scale; feature rates and tone. Thousands more accounts archived at nderf.org.
studies.cite: Long J, Perry P. Evidence of the Afterlife: The Science of Near-Death Experiences. HarperOne, 2010.
studies.nature: Self-selected internet survey: people who went looking for an NDE website, answering retrospectively in English with no medical records. The percentages describe self-identified experiencers, not people who nearly died.

studies.name: Liège narratives
studies.finding: 154 written NDE narratives analysed for which features occur and in what order; no fixed sequence was found.
studies.cite: Martial C et al. Temporality of features in near-death experience narratives. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 2017;11:311.
studies.nature: Recruited from the same Coma Science Group and IANDS pool as the distressing narratives on this map, so the two bubbles overlap rather than confirm each other.

studies.name: Indian cases
studies.finding: 16 cases investigated in north India: messengers called yamdoots, a clerk with a book of records, and being sent back because the wrong person was brought. Beings of light were reported here, unlike in Pasricha's later south Indian series. A quarter woke with residual marks on the body from being branded in the other realm. No tunnel and no life review in any case.
studies.cite: Pasricha S, Stevenson I. Near-death experiences in India: a preliminary report. Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease 1986;174:165-70.
studies.type_label: Summoned by mistake and sent back

walk.label: The yamdoots come
walk.text: Messengers called yamdoots arrive and take the person away, sometimes roughly. They are the servants of Yama, lord of the dead.

walk.label: The man with the book
walk.text: The person is brought before Chitragupta, 'the man with the book', who keeps the record of what each life contains.

walk.label: The wrong person
walk.text: The book is checked and a mistake is found. Ninety-four per cent of the Indian cases are sent back because of such an error; in a third, somebody else died instead.

walk.label: Beings of light
walk.text: Beings of light were reported by the north Indian experiencers. Pasricha's later south Indian series reported none, which is one of the few differences inside one country.

walk.label: Sent back, and marked
walk.text: They are sent back, often against their wish. A quarter wake with residual marks on the body where they were branded in the other realm. No case reports a tunnel or a life review.

studies.name: Life After Life interviews
studies.finding: About 150 interviews that named the phenomenon and listed its recurring elements.
studies.cite: Moody R. Life After Life. Mockingbird Books, 1975.

studies.name: Life at Death
studies.finding: 102 people who came close to death; the five-stage model (peace, body separation, darkness, light, entering the light).
studies.cite: Ring K. Life at Death: A Scientific Investigation of the Near-Death Experience. Coward, McCann & Geoghegan, 1980.

studies.name: Distressing narratives
studies.finding: 123 accounts from Liege scored 7 or more on the Greyson scale; 17 of them (14%) were distressing: 8 inverse, 8 hellish, 1 void. They do not differ from the other 106 on the transcendental features, the light and the other world score the same, only on the affective ones, where the median falls from 6 to 2. Six of the 17 begin with peace before turning.
studies.cite: Cassol H, Martial C, Annen J, et al. A systematic analysis of distressing near-death experience accounts. Memory 2019;27:1122-29.
studies.scene_note: Peace and light are present in this walk because the paper found them present: what collapses in a distressing experience is the feeling, not the content. Six of the seventeen accounts open with peace or joy.
studies.nature: The 17 come from a coma and intensive-care subgroup of the Liege pool, so the 14% is not a general rate. This cohort overlaps the 154 Liege narratives on the map; the two bubbles are not independent samples.

walk.label: It can begin well
walk.text: Six of the seventeen distressing accounts clearly mention positive feelings at the beginning: peacefulness, or joy. Then it turns.

walk.label: The dark
walk.text: Darkness, which in the one void account is where the experience stays: an endless emptiness with nobody in it.

walk.label: The light is still there
walk.text: These accounts do not differ from the other 106 on the transcendental features. The bright light and the other world score the same. What collapses is the feeling.

walk.label: Presences
walk.text: Eight of the accounts are inverse, where the usual features arrive but feel hostile or wrong. Eight are hellish, with a place of torment.

walk.label: A place of torment
walk.text: On the affective component of the Greyson scale the median falls from six to two. The content is the same; the experience of it is not.

studies.name: NDERF overview of elements
studies.finding: A 1999 NDERF web page listing the elements its editors see recurring, including unusual sounds: 'pleasant, musical, buzzing or ringing'. It publishes no percentages and is an advocacy page rather than research, so it is cited here only for the wording of the sounds element and is kept off the map.
studies.cite: Long J. NDE overview. Near Death Experience Research Foundation website, 1999 (archived).
studies.no_walk: A website overview rather than a study. Nothing is measured, so there is nothing to walk.

studies.name: Tibetan delok accounts
studies.place: Tibetan cultural world (texts at Dharamsala; interviews in Bhutan and Nepal)
studies.finding: Deloks ('those who return from the hereafter') are people taken for dead who revive and describe a journey through the Buddhist realms. Bailey compared these accounts with Western NDEs: no tunnel, and the reckoning is public rather than private, a bridge, a scale with black pebbles for sinful deeds against white, and the mirror of existence. They come back carrying a message for the living.
studies.cite: Bailey LW. A 'little death': the near-death experience and Tibetan delogs. Journal of Near-Death Studies 2001;19:139-59. The count of 16 accounts (12 texts from the Library of Tibetan Works and Archives, 4 interviews by Francoise Pommaret) is Kellehear's tally, not Bailey's.
studies.type_label: A guided tour of the realms
studies.nature: Kellehear includes the deloks only 'for the sake of completeness': some had dyings on fasting days, the 10th, 15th and 30th of each month, and local observers took them for epileptics. Bailey's own named case is Sangs Rgyas Chos 'dzom, a twelve-year-old girl in Bhutan shortly after 1650.

walk.label: Taken for dead
walk.text: A delok, 'one who returns from the hereafter', is taken for dead, sometimes for days. Most of them are women.

walk.label: Guided through the realms
walk.text: Guides lead them through the Buddhist realms, hot and cold. Kellehear records no mention of a tunnel in any of these accounts.

walk.label: Weighed in public
walk.text: The reckoning is public, not a private replay: a small black demon holds black pebbles for the sinful deeds, a white deity holds white pebbles to weigh against them.

walk.label: The bridge, the scale, the mirror
walk.text: They watch the judgment of souls with a bridge, a scale, and the mirror of existence, in which what was done is shown.

walk.label: Sent back with a message
walk.text: They are judged and given a message to carry back, usually to practise faithfully and to stop causing harm. One twelve-year-old Bhutanese delok's task was to be a messenger between the living and the dead.

studies.name: The Myth of Er
studies.finding: The oldest surviving Western narrative of this shape. Er, a soldier killed in battle, revives on his funeral pyre on the twelfth day and describes leaving the body, a journey to a place of judgment, a pillar of light 'straight as a column, extending right through the whole heaven and through the earth', souls choosing their next lives, and being appointed to carry the report back. He could not say how he returned to the body.
studies.cite: Plato. Republic, Book X, c. 380 BC. Benjamin Jowett translation.
studies.type_label: Appointed a witness and sent back
studies.nature: Plato tells this as a tale, not a case report: 'this too is a tale of a hero, Er the son of Armenius, a Pamphylian by birth.' Pinned in Pamphylia because that is where Plato puts Er; the Republic was written in Athens.

walk.label: Slain in battle
walk.text: Er is killed in battle. Ten days later his body is found undecayed. When his soul left the body he went on a journey with a great company.

walk.label: Two openings in the earth
walk.text: They reach a place where two openings gape in the earth and two in the heaven above it, with judges seated in the space between.

walk.label: The judges
walk.text: The just are sent to the right and upward, the unjust to the left and down. Souls come up dusty and worn, or down clean and bright.

walk.label: Seven days in the meadow
walk.text: They go forth into the meadow and encamp as at a festival. Those who know one another embrace, and each asks the others what they saw.

walk.label: The pillar of light
walk.text: Four days on they see from above a line of light, straight as a column, running through the whole heaven and earth, like the rainbow but brighter and purer.

walk.label: Appointed the messenger
walk.text: He is told he is to be the messenger who carries the report to men. How he returned to the body he could not say. He revives on the funeral pyre.

studies.name: Gregory the Great's Dialogues
studies.finding: Four accounts in Book IV of people taken for dead who revived. In the best known, Stephen is told he was summoned by mistake, the wrong man of the same name, and is sent back: the same clerical-error motif found in Indian cases fourteen centuries later. Gregory is blunt that it did Stephen no good, 'he did never perfectly amend his former wicked life', and he died again in the Roman plague of 590.
studies.cite: Gregory the Great. Dialogues, Book IV, chapters 32 and 37, c. 593. Gardner edition, 1911. Discussed in Zaleski C, Otherworld Journeys, Oxford University Press, 1987.
studies.type_label: Summoned by mistake and sent back
studies.scene_note: Pinned at Rome, where Gregory wrote. The four accounts are set in three places: the desert of Evasa, Constantinople, and Rome.

walk.label: Stephen dies in Constantinople
walk.text: Stephen, in Constantinople on business, falls sick and dies. His soul is carried to the dungeon of hell and he is brought before a judge.

walk.label: The wrong Stephen
walk.text: The judge refuses him: 'I commanded not this man to be brought, but Stephen the smith.' He revives, and the smith next door dies at that same hour.

walk.label: A soldier dies in the plague
walk.text: A soldier at the point of death has his soul carried out of his body so that he lies void of all sense and feeling, then comes quickly to himself again.

walk.label: The bridge and the black river
walk.text: He sees a bridge under which a black and smoky river runs, with a filthy and intolerable smell.

walk.label: Crossing
walk.text: The unjust slip from the bridge into the stink below. The just pass over it unhindered to the far side.

walk.label: Green meadows beyond
walk.text: On the farther side are pleasant green meadows full of sweet flowers, with companies of men walking in them, all apparelled in white.

walk.label: The house built of gold
walk.text: Mansions stand shining with brightness and light, one of them sumptuous, its bricks seeming to be of gold, and old men, young, girls and boys carry them to the building.

walk.label: Stephen on the bridge
walk.text: On the same bridge he sees Stephen again, drawn by the legs downward by terrible men out of the river and pulled upward by the arms by white and beautiful persons.

walk.label: Sent back, and unchanged
walk.text: The soldier returns and tells what he saw. Gregory records that Stephen never perfectly amended his life, and died years later in the plague.

studies.name: The Vision of Drythelm
studies.finding: A Northumbrian householder died of illness, revived at dawn, and described leaving the body and being led by a guide 'with a countenance full of light, and shining raiment' through places of punishment and of light, then sent back. He divided his property in three and lived as a monk at Melrose afterwards. Bede wrote it down about 731, thirty-five years later, from Haemgils, who had questioned him at Melrose.
studies.cite: Bede. Ecclesiastical History of the English People, Book V, Chapter XII; event dated c. 696, written c. 731. Revised A. M. Sellar translation, 1907. Discussed in Zaleski C, Otherworld Journeys, Oxford University Press, 1987.
studies.type_label: A guided tour of the realms
studies.nature: Pinned at Melrose, the one place in the account that is certainly identified. Bede's 'Incuneningum' has never been agreed on: Cunninghame in Ayrshire, Tyninghame in East Lothian and Chester-le-Street have all been proposed.

walk.label: Dead at nightfall
walk.text: He dies in the beginning of the night and comes to life again at dawn, sitting suddenly up. Only his wife stays with him. A guide with a countenance full of light and shining raiment leads him away.

walk.label: The valley of flame and hail
walk.text: A broad deep valley of infinite length: one side terrible with raging flames, the other with violent hail and cold snows, and souls tossed from one side to the other as by a storm.

walk.label: The pit, and the tongs
walk.text: The shadows thicken until he can see nothing but the darkness and his guide. Globes of black flame rise from a pit and fall back into it, and laughing spirits come at him with tongs.

walk.label: Out into clear light
walk.text: His guide returns, the spirits scatter, and he is brought out of the darkness into an atmosphere of clear light, brighter than the noontide sun.

walk.label: A wall with no door
walk.text: A vast wall stands before them, boundless in length and height, with no door, window or way up. At the wall they are suddenly on top of it.

walk.label: The flowery field
walk.text: Beyond the wall is a wide and pleasant plain full of fragrant flowers, with companies of men in white. He thinks this might be the kingdom of heaven. His guide answers his unspoken thought: it is not.

walk.label: A brighter light still, and singing
walk.text: Farther on he sees a light far more beautiful than before, hears sweet singing, and smells so wonderful a fragrance that the flowery field now seems mean by comparison.

walk.label: Sent back to live differently
walk.text: He is not allowed in. He returns and tells his wife he must not live as he was wont, divides his property in three, and takes the tonsure at Melrose.

studies.name: The Vision of Tundale
studies.finding: An Irish knight from Cashel collapses at table in Cork, 'struck by I know not what sudden cause', and lies as dead from the tenth hour of Wednesday to the tenth hour of Saturday. Demons set on his soul before his guardian angel reaches him, and he is led through the otherworld undergoing the torments himself rather than only watching. Written down by Marcus, an Irish monk at Regensburg; one of the most widely copied of the medieval otherworld journeys, translated forty-three times into fifteen languages by the fifteenth century.
studies.cite: Marcus of Regensburg. Visio Tnugdali, vision dated 1148, composed shortly after. Wagner critical edition, 1882. Discussed in Zaleski C, Otherworld Journeys, Oxford University Press, 1987.
studies.type_label: A guided tour of the realms
studies.nature: Every surviving manuscript reads 1149, which Wagner shows is an old copying error: the text's own synchronisms, including the death of St Malachy at Clairvaux, fix the vision in 1148.

walk.label: Struck down at table
walk.text: Reaching for his food he cannot bring his hand back to his mouth. He cries out, hands his axe to his companion's wife and says: guard my axe, for I am dying.

walk.label: Three days as dead
walk.text: He lies dead from the tenth hour of Wednesday to the tenth hour of Saturday. Those who palpated the body felt a slight warmth in the left breast, so burial was delayed.

walk.label: The angel like a bright star
walk.text: Demons set on the soul. Then he sees something coming from far off like a most shining star. It greets him by his own name: Hail, Tnugdal, what are you doing?

walk.label: He suffers the torments himself
walk.text: He is not only shown the punishments but undergoes very many incredible and intolerable kinds of them. The angel tells him it followed him from birth and he never took its counsel.

walk.label: The plank across the valley
walk.text: A plank reaches from one mountain to another like a bridge, a thousand paces long and one foot wide. He sees many fall from it; only a pilgrim priest crosses unhurt.

walk.label: The bridge of nails
walk.text: A second plank, two miles long and a palm wide, is set with the sharpest iron nails that pierce the feet of everyone crossing. Below is a lake of bellowing beasts asking only for souls.

walk.label: The silver wall
walk.text: A very high and bright wall of silver, with no gate in it, which divine power brings him through. Inside are choirs of saints rejoicing.

walk.label: The wall of purest gold
walk.text: A second wall as high as the first, of the purest and most brilliant gold, so that the shine of the metal alone delights more than everything seen before it.

walk.label: He revives before the crowd
walk.text: He comes back to his body in front of the clergy and the crowd gathered to bury him.

studies.name: Beaufort's drowning
studies.finding: Francis Beaufort, then a midshipman of 17, fell into Portsmouth harbour and nearly drowned. His account, written in 1825 and published in 1847, describes no pain, calm, and 'every incident of my past life' passing before him: the first detailed first-person life review in English.
studies.cite: Beaufort F. Letter to Dr W. H. Wollaston, written 1825, published 1847.
studies.type_label: Calm and a life review, without a journey

studies.name: Heim's falls
studies.finding: The first systematic collection. Albert Heim, a geologist, survived a fall in the Alps and spent 25 years gathering accounts from climbers, soldiers and workers who had fallen. He found about 95% felt no pain or fear, but calm, speeded thought and a review of their lives.
studies.cite: Heim A. Notizen uber den Tod durch Absturz. Jahrbuch des Schweizer Alpenclub 1892;27:327-37. Translated by Noyes R, Kletti R, Omega 1972;3:45-52.
studies.type_label: Calm and a life review, without a journey

studies.name: Otherworld Journeys
studies.finding: The scholarly comparison of medieval and modern accounts. Zaleski found the constants (leaving the body, a guide, a barrier, a return with a changed life) and the differences: medieval journeys are guided tours with judgment and punishment, modern ones are private, warm and without hell.
studies.cite: Zaleski C. Otherworld Journeys: Accounts of Near-Death Experience in Medieval and Modern Times. Oxford University Press, 1987.
studies.scene_note: Zaleski's constants rendered as a walk: what medieval and modern accounts share is leaving the body, a guide or companion, another place, a barrier, and a return that changes the life. What they do not share, hell and judgment on one side, warmth and privacy on the other, is left out.

studies.name: Tangshan earthquake survivors
studies.finding: 81 survivors of the 1976 earthquake that killed about 240,000 people were interviewed eleven years after it; 32 (40%) scored 7 or more on the Greyson scale. Most were cognitive or transcendental in type. Item by item, a life review was the second commonest feature at 51%, leaving the body 43%, a tunnel-like dark region 16% and an unnaturally brilliant light 15%.
studies.cite: Feng Z, Liu J. Near-death experiences among survivors of the 1976 Tangshan earthquake. Journal of Near-Death Studies 1992;11:39-48.
studies.scene_note: Stage strengths here are not the published item rates: Feng and Liu report a life review in 51% of the 32, leaving the body in 43%, a tunnel-like dark region in 16% and a brilliant light in 15%. Kellehear cautions that the tunnel item was offered to respondents as a category rather than volunteered.

studies.name: The first medical account
studies.finding: A French military physician recorded an apothecary who, after heavy bleeding for a fever, lay unconscious and on waking described 'a light so pure and strong he thought he was in paradise', the most pleasant sensation of his life. The oldest known description by a doctor, rediscovered in 2014.
studies.cite: du Monchaux PJ. Anecdotes de Medecine, 1740. Rediscovered by Charlier P, Resuscitation 2014;85:e155.
studies.scene_note: A single case, with no percentages: the patient described losing all sensation and then a light so pure and strong he thought he was in paradise. Only those two stages are shown, because only those two are in the account.
studies.type_label: Calm and a light, without a journey

studies.name: Chamorro cases, Guam
studies.finding: Four Chamorro accounts from Guam, two interviewed by Green himself. No tunnel, no life review. People report leaving the body, flying 'through the clouds' or walking on a road, invisible visits to living relatives in America, and arriving at a gardenlike paradise where they are met by the dead, some of them relatives.
studies.cite: Green JT. Near-death experiences in a Chammorro culture. Vital Signs 1984;4(1-2):6-7. Not digitised; every detail here is as summarised in Kellehear A, Census of non-Western near-death experiences to 2005. Journal of Near-Death Studies 2008;26:249-65.
studies.type_label: A journey across a familiar landscape
studies.nature: Green's original newsletter article is not available anywhere online; this entry rests entirely on Kellehear's summaries of it.

walk.label: Out of the body
walk.text: The Chamorro accounts begin with leaving the body, which is unusual among the non-Western cases: India and China's do not report it.

walk.label: Flying, or walking on a road
walk.text: People recount flying through the clouds, or suddenly finding themselves walking on a road. Some make invisible visits to living relatives in America.

walk.label: Met in a gardenlike place
walk.text: They arrive at a paradisiacal place of gardenlike appearance and are met there by the dead, some of whom are relatives.

walk.label: Back again
walk.text: They return. There is no tunnel in any of the four accounts and no review of the life. Green's own article has never been digitised; this is as Kellehear summarises it.

studies.name: A Maori account
studies.finding: A Maori woman's account recorded by Michael King. She hovers over her own head, leaves the room and flies north over the Waikato, the Manukau and the lands of Ngati Whatua, Ngapuhi, Te Rarawa and Te Aupouri to Te Rerenga Wairua, 'the leaping off place of spirits' at Cape Reinga. A voice stops her there, telling her her time had not come, and she wakes to her living relatives at the bedside. No tunnel, no life review.
studies.cite: King M. Being Pakeha: An Encounter with New Zealand and the Maori Renaissance, 1985, pp. 92-94. Quoted in Kellehear A, An Hawaiian near-death experience. Journal of Near-Death Studies 2001;20:31-35.
studies.type_label: A journey across a familiar landscape

walk.label: Hovering over her own head
walk.text: In her spirit she hovers over her own head, then leaves the room.

walk.label: North, over the named land
walk.text: She travels north towards the Tail of the Fish, passing over the Waikato River, across the Manukau, over Ngati Whatua, Ngapuhi, Te Rarawa and Te Aupouri.

walk.label: Te Rerenga Wairua
walk.text: She reaches Te Rerenga Wairua, the leaping off place of spirits at Cape Reinga. She performs ablutions, climbs a ledge and dances before the entrance to the underworld.

walk.label: A voice turns her back
walk.text: A voice stops her and tells her that her time has not come, and that she must return until she is called again. She wakes to her anxious living relatives.

studies.name: A Hawaiian account
studies.finding: Kalima, a woman in Kona, in an account from the early 1900s found in a 1907 collection of Hawaiian folk tales: the spirit leaves the body, travels, is met and sent back. Like the Maori and Chamorro cases it has a journey and deceased relatives but no tunnel and no life review, and no mention of light or darkness at all.
studies.cite: Kellehear A. An Hawaiian near-death experience. Journal of Near-Death Studies 2001;20:31-35.
studies.type_label: A journey across a familiar landscape

walk.label: The spirit leaves
walk.text: Kalima, a woman in Kona, in an account recorded in a 1907 collection of Hawaiian folk tales: her spirit leaves the body.

walk.label: The journey
walk.text: She travels. There is no mention anywhere in the account of light or of darkness, which sets it apart from the Western pattern.

walk.label: Met by the dead
walk.text: She is met by deceased people, as in the Maori and Chamorro accounts. There is no tunnel and no review of her life.

walk.label: Sent back
walk.text: She is sent back and revives.

studies.name: Census of non-Western accounts
studies.finding: A review of every non-Western NDE account published to 2005, restricted to experiences associated with illness. Two features recur everywhere: travelling to another realm, and meeting the dead. The tunnel is absent from the Indian, Tibetan, Chamorro, Native North American and Aboriginal Australian accounts and questionable elsewhere; Kellehear's conclusion is that 'there is no actual tunnel in near-death experiences', only darkness described differently by different cultures. The life review is largely confined to societies with a dominant historic religion.
studies.cite: Kellehear A. Census of non-Western near-death experiences to 2005: overview of the current data. Journal of Near-Death Studies 2008;26:249-65.
studies.scene_note: This is the census's own conclusion rendered as a walk: across every non-Western account published to 2005, two things recur, travelling to another realm and meeting the dead. The tunnel and the life review are left out because neither is cross-cultural, not because no account has them.

studies.name: Soviet resuscitation and 'clinical death'
studies.finding: Vladimir Negovsky founded reanimatology and ran front-line resuscitation teams in the Second World War, reviving more than 40 wounded men, some clinically dead from blood loss. He named 'clinical death', the reversible period without circulation. Mass survival of clinical death is what made modern NDE research possible; his own work did not record the experiences.
studies.cite: Negovsky VA, work from 1943 onward; see Safar P, Vladimir A. Negovsky, the father of reanimatology. Resuscitation 2002;53:111-13.
studies.no_walk: Negovsky revived people but did not record what they experienced. Nothing here to walk, and inventing one would be a lie about his work.

studies.name: Brazilian research
studies.place: Juiz de Fora and Sao Paulo, Brazil
studies.finding: Brazil has the largest Spiritist population in the world and a long research tradition into mediumship, out-of-body and near-death experiences, centred on NUPES at the Federal University of Juiz de Fora. The largest relevant survey, Monteiro de Barros and colleagues, asked 1,053 Brazilians about sixteen spiritual and religious experiences including near-death ones: 92% reported at least one in their lifetime and half had felt the presence of a dead person. The paper is paywalled and its near-death figure is not in the abstract, so this atlas has no Brazilian near-death rate to show. A single Brazilian case scored on the Greyson scale is published in open access.
studies.cite: Monteiro de Barros MC et al. Prevalence of spiritual and religious experiences in the general population: a Brazilian nationwide study. Transcultural Psychiatry 2025;62:422-36. Case report: Braghetta CC et al. Trends in Psychiatry and Psychotherapy 2013;35:81-4.
studies.no_walk: A survey of spiritual and religious experiences rather than a near-death study, and the near-death figure inside it is behind a paywall. Nothing to walk until a Brazilian rate is published openly.
studies.nature: An online convenience sample of 1,053 people, so 'nationwide' in reach but not a population prevalence the way a household survey would be.

studies.name: Enkidu's dream of the House of the Dust
studies.nature: A dream, told by a dying man inside a poem. Enkidu does not go and come back: the dream says the road has no returning, and he dies in the next tablet. The thing that seizes him has a dark face and a lion's claws; what its face is likened to is broken away in the tablet, so nothing more is built here.
studies.type_label: A guided tour of the realms
studies.finding: Enkidu tells Gilgamish a dream: the firmament roared, and a man with a dark face and nails like a lion's claws bore down on him and led him by the road on which there is no returning, down to the Dwelling of Darkness. There the dead sit in the dark wearing a garment of feathers, with dust for food and mud for sustenance. The tablet breaks off as the Recorder of Hades lifts her head and looks at him.
studies.cite: Epic of Gilgamish, Tablet VII, column IV. R. Campbell Thompson translation, 1928.

walk.label: The firmament roared
walk.text: The firmament roared and the earth echoed it. He stood by himself. Then he saw a man, all dark was his face, and his nails like the claws of a lion.

walk.label: Pressed down
walk.text: His hands became like a bird's. The figure overcame him, climbed up and pressed him down, and he could not throw the weight off his body.

walk.label: The road of no returning
walk.text: He is led to the Dwelling of Darkness, the home of Irkalla, the dwelling from which whoever enters comes forth never, by the road on the passage whereof there can be no returning.

walk.label: At the gate the crown is humbled
walk.text: At the gate the crown is humbled: those who wore crowns and of old ruled over the country have been brought low here.

walk.label: The House of the Dust
walk.text: In the House of the Dust their food is dust and the mud is their sustenance. Bird-like they wear a garment of feathers, and sitting there in the darkness they will never see the light.

walk.label: Who sits there
walk.text: High priest and acolyte are sitting there, seer and magician, the priest who anointed the Sea of the great gods. Etana and Sumuqan sit there, and Ereshkigal, Queen of the Underworld.

walk.label: The Recorder of Hades
walk.text: Belit-seri, Recorder of Hades, bows before Ereshkigal and reads aloud before her. She lifts her head and beholds him. Here the tablet breaks off.

studies.name: The weighing of the heart
studies.nature: A funerary text, not an experience. Nobody nearly died, nobody returned, and there is no event behind it. It is on this map because it is the oldest surviving description of the shape, not because anyone reported it.
studies.type_label: A guided tour of the realms
studies.finding: Not a report by anyone but a liturgy, spoken in the first person by the dead scribe Ani. Anubis holds the door and asks its name. Forty-two gods sit in a row in the Hall of Double Right and Truth. The heart is weighed against the feather of law while Thoth stands by with a reed-pen and a palette of black and red ink, and Am-mit the Devourer waits behind him. Found true, Ani is led by the hand to a homestead for ever.
studies.cite: The Book of the Dead, Chapter CXXV and the judgment scene, Plates III-IV. E. A. Wallis Budge translation of the Papyrus of Ani, 1895. The forty-two denials are in Budge's appendix, not in Ani's own text.

walk.label: The door asks its own name
walk.text: Anubis holds the door. Do you know the name of this door, to declare it to me? Driven away of Shu is the name of this door. Pass, for you know the names.

walk.label: Where nothing grows
walk.text: I have drawn near to the place where the acacia tree grows not, where the tree thick with leaves exists not, and where the ground yields neither herb nor grass.

walk.label: Forty-two in a row
walk.text: Forty-two gods sit in a row in the middle of the Hall of Double Right and Truth, and he must know the name of every one of them.

walk.label: The denials
walk.text: He denies each deed in turn. I have not committed murder. I have not filched that which has been offered in the temples. I have not snatched the milk from the mouth of the babe.

walk.label: A word to his own heart
walk.text: My heart my mother, my heart my coming into being. May there be no parting of you from me in the presence of him who keeps the scales.

walk.label: The weighing
walk.text: The heart goes into one pan of the Great Balance against the feather of law. Anubis, jackal-headed, tests the tongue of the scales.

walk.label: Thoth writes it down
walk.text: Thoth stands with his reed-pen and a palette of black and red ink to record the result, then declares it: found true by trial in the Great Balance, no wickedness found in him.

walk.label: The Devourer waits
walk.text: Behind Thoth waits Am-mit, the eater of the dead, part crocodile, part hippopotamus, part lion. Let it not be given to the devourer to prevail over him.

walk.label: A homestead for ever
walk.text: Horus takes Ani by the hand and leads him to Osiris, lord of eternity, who grants him a homestead for ever in Sekhet-hetepu, with wheat and barley for it.

studies.name: Odysseus among the dead
studies.nature: A living man's journey, by ship, with a crew and sheep. His mother says it in the text: how did you come down here while you are still alive. He does not descend; the dead come up to him. There is no tunnel and no light.
studies.finding: Odysseus sails to where the river Oceanus meets the land of the Cimmerians, digs a trench a cubit each way and pours honey, milk, wine and water. The dead come up to him across it and he guards the blood with a drawn sword. He speaks with Elpenor, with Teiresias, and with his own mother, who asks how a living man came down. Three times he springs to hold her and three times she slips away. He is driven back by fear that the Gorgon's head will be sent up.
studies.cite: Homer, Odyssey, Book XI. Samuel Butler translation, Project Gutenberg.

walk.label: Into the deep waters of Oceanus
walk.text: They reach the deep waters of the river Oceanus, and the land and city of the Cimmerians, who live enshrouded in mist and darkness which the rays of the sun never pierce.

walk.label: A trench a cubit each way
walk.text: He draws his sword and digs the trench a cubit each way, and makes a drink-offering to all the dead: honey and milk, then wine, then water, with white barley meal sprinkled over the whole.

walk.label: They come trooping up
walk.text: The ghosts come trooping up from Erebus with a strange screaming: brides, young bachelors, old men worn out with toil, and brave men killed in battle with their armour still smirched with blood.

walk.label: Elpenor, unburied
walk.text: Elpenor, who fell from Circe's roof and lies unburied, asks for a barrow on the sea shore with the oar he used to row with planted over the grave.

walk.label: Teiresias drinks the blood
walk.text: Teiresias comes with his golden sceptre: withdraw your sword that I may drink of the blood and answer your questions truly. He foretells that death shall come from the sea.

walk.label: How did you come down alive?
walk.text: His mother Anticlea asks how he came down to this abode of darkness while he is still alive, for between them and the living are great and terrible waters, and Oceanus, which no man can cross on foot.

walk.label: Three times she slips away
walk.text: Three times he springs towards her to clasp her in his arms, and each time she flits from his embrace as it were a dream or a phantom. The soul flits away as though it were a dream.

walk.label: The meadow of asphodel
walk.text: Achilles, who says he would rather be a paid servant in a poor man's house and be above ground than king of kings among the dead, strides off across a meadow full of asphodel.

walk.label: Minos gives sentence
walk.text: Minos sits with his golden sceptre in the spacious house of Hades, giving judgment on the dead, and the ghosts gather round him sitting and standing to learn his sentences on them.

walk.label: Tityus, Tantalus, Sisyphus
walk.text: Two vultures dig their beaks into Tityus's liver. Tantalus stands in a lake up to his chin that dries up whenever he stoops to drink. Sisyphus's pitiless stone comes thundering down to the plain.

walk.label: Driven back
walk.text: So many thousands of ghosts crowd round him with appalling cries that he is panic stricken lest the Gorgon's head be sent up from the house of Hades, and he hastens back to his ship.

studies.name: Nachiketa and Yama
studies.nature: A living boy, given away by his father's word, not summoned and not dying. The Upanishad describes no place at all: no gate, no river, no light, no landscape. Yama's dwelling is called only 'my house', so nothing is built here. The Upanishad also never narrates the return; only the older Brahmana telling does.
studies.finding: Asked a third time to whom he will be given, Nachiketa's father answers in anger: I shall give you to Death. He goes, and Yama is not at home. He waits three nights in the house without eating, and because a Brahmana guest enters a house like fire, Yama on his return owes him three boons. The first is that his father be free from anger and know him when Death has dismissed him.
studies.cite: Katha Upanishad, First Adhyaya, First Valli. F. Max Muller translation, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15, 1884. The return itself is in Taittiriya Brahmana III.11.8, which Muller quotes in his introduction.

walk.label: I shall give you to Death
walk.text: He asks his father a second and a third time to whom he will be given. Then the father replies, in anger: I shall give you to Death.

walk.label: At the head of many
walk.text: I go as the first, at the head of many who have still to die. I go in the midst of many who are now dying. What will be the work of Yama which today he has to do to me?

walk.label: Nobody is home
walk.text: He reaches the house while Yama is away, and no one receives him. A voice warns: fire enters into the houses when a Brahmana enters as a guest. Bring water.

walk.label: Three nights without eating
walk.text: Yama returns and finds the boy has dwelt three nights in his house without eating. O Brahmana, as you have done so, choose now three boons. Hail to you, and welfare to me.

walk.label: The first boon
walk.text: I choose that my father be pacified, kind and free from anger towards me, and that he may know me and greet me when I shall have been dismissed by you.

walk.label: The second boon
walk.text: In the heaven-world there is no fear. You are not there, O Death, and no one is afraid on account of old age. Leaving behind both hunger and thirst, and out of reach of sorrow, all rejoice.

walk.label: The third boon, and the doubt
walk.text: There is that doubt when a man is dead: some saying he is, others he is not. This I should like to know, taught by you. This is the third of my boons.

walk.label: Death tries to buy him off
walk.text: Choose sons and grandsons who shall live a hundred years, herds of cattle, elephants, gold and horses. Take these fair maidens with their chariots and musical instruments. But do not ask me about dying.

walk.label: He refuses, and asks to go home
walk.text: Keep your horses, keep dance and song for yourself. In the older Brahmana telling he is asked what he ate on each of the three nights: your offspring, your cattle, your good works. Then: may I return living to my father.

studies.name: Aristeas of Proconnesos
studies.nature: Reported at second hand, with the historian's own distance kept: they say that Aristeas. Nothing in Herodotus says his soul left his body; soul-flight is a modern reading, not in the text. Nor does he visit any land of the dead: the Arimaspeia is an overland journey north under Apollo's possession.
studies.type_label: A body missing, and a man seen again
studies.finding: Aristeas, in birth inferior to none of the citizens, walked into a fuller's shop in Proconnesos and died there. A man from Artake disputed it, saying he had met him on the road to Kyzicos and spoken with him. When the shop was opened he was not found there either dead or alive. In the seventh year he appeared again and composed the Arimaspeia.
studies.cite: Herodotus, Histories IV.13-16. G. C. Macaulay translation, Project Gutenberg.

walk.label: Dead in a fuller's shop
walk.text: Aristeas, in birth inferior to none of the citizens, entered a fuller's shop in Proconnesos and there died. The fuller closed his workshop and went to report the matter.

walk.label: But he was seen on the road
walk.text: A man of Kyzicos who had come from Artake entered into controversy with those who said so, and declared that he had met him going towards Kyzicos and had spoken with him.

walk.label: Neither dead nor alive
walk.text: The relatives came to the shop with the things proper for burial. When the house was opened, Aristeas was not found there either dead or alive.

walk.label: In the seventh year
walk.text: In the seventh year after this he appeared at Proconnesos and composed the verses the Greeks now call the Arimaspeia. Having composed them, he disappeared a second time.

walk.label: What the verses say
walk.text: In them he came to the land of the Issedonians, being possessed by Phoebus. Beyond them dwelt the one-eyed Arimaspians, beyond those the gold-guarding griffins, and beyond them the Hyperboreans, as far as the sea.

walk.label: Two hundred and forty years later
walk.text: He appeared in Metapontion and told them to set up an altar of Apollo, saying that he had accompanied the god, being then a raven. Having said this he disappeared.

studies.name: Zalmoxis and the cellar
studies.place: Lands of the Getai, lower Danube (now Romania and Bulgaria)
studies.finding: Herodotus relays what Greeks on the Hellespont told him: Zalmoxis feasted the chief men of the Getai and taught them that they would not die but come to a place where they would have all things good. Meanwhile he was digging himself a chamber under the ground. He went down into it and lived there three years; the Thracians mourned him as dead; in the fourth year he appeared again, and what he had told them became credible.
studies.cite: Herodotus, Histories IV.94-96. G. C. Macaulay translation, Project Gutenberg.
studies.type_label: A death staged, and a return
studies.nature: On this telling nobody returns from death: the chamber is a cellar Zalmoxis dug himself, and the story is a debunking. Herodotus attributes it to Greek informants and then withholds belief: of this matter and the chamber under ground, I neither disbelieve it nor do I very strongly believe.

walk.label: A messenger on three javelins
walk.text: Every fourth year the Getai cast lots and send one of themselves as a messenger to Salmoxis, charged with their requests. They swing him up and throw him so as to fall on the spear-points.

walk.label: What he taught them
walk.text: He prepared a banqueting-hall and feasted the chief men of the tribe, instructing them that neither he nor his guests nor their descendants would die, but would come to a place where they would live for ever and have all things good.

walk.label: The chamber under the ground
walk.text: Meanwhile he was making a chamber for himself under the ground. When it was finished he disappeared from among the Thracians and went down into it, and continued to live there for three years.

walk.label: They mourned him as dead
walk.text: The Thracians missed him. They grieved for his loss and mourned for him as dead.

walk.label: In the fourth year
walk.text: Then in the fourth year he appeared to the Thracians again, and in this way the things which Salmoxis said became credible to them.

walk.label: The historian's doubt
walk.text: As to this matter and the chamber under ground, writes Herodotus, I neither disbelieve it nor do I very strongly believe, but I think that this Salmoxis lived many years before Pythagoras.

studies.name: Thespesius of Soli
studies.nature: Told inside a philosophical dialogue, and the text itself denies he was fully dead: his kinsman tells him he is not in the number of the dead as yet, having come with his intellectual faculty only and left the rest of his soul, like an anchor, in his body.
studies.type_label: A guided tour of the realms
studies.finding: Thespesius fell headlong from a precipice, broke nothing, but the fall beat the breath out of him. Three days later, as they were letting him down into the grave, he came to himself. He describes being flung from the helm into open sea, souls rising as little fiery bubbles that break open into men and women, three lakes of boiling gold, freezing lead and scaly iron, and his own father climbing out of an abyss covered in scars.
studies.cite: Plutarch, Concerning Such Whom God Is Slow to Punish, section 22, in Plutarch's Morals, William W. Goodwin edition. Project Gutenberg.

walk.label: The fall
walk.text: He fell from a precipice upon his neck. He received no wound and broke no limb, but the force of the fall beat the breath out of his body. Three days later they carried him out to be buried.

walk.label: Flung from the helm
walk.text: When his sense first left his body it seemed to him as if he were a pilot flung from the helm by the force of a storm into the midst of the sea. Then he rose again above water by degrees.

walk.label: Stars of vast magnitude
walk.text: He saw stars of a vast magnitude, at immense distances from one another, sending forth a light wonderful for the brightness of its colour, which shot itself out in length with incredible force.

walk.label: Riding the light
walk.text: The soul rode on that light as if in a chariot, and was most swiftly, yet as gently and smoothly, dandled from one place to another.

walk.label: Souls like fiery bubbles
walk.text: He saw the souls of the newly departed mounting from below, resembling little fiery bubbles to which the air gave way. The bubbles broke by degrees, and out came men and women, light and nimble.

walk.label: Not dead yet
walk.text: A kinsman who died very young greets him by a new name: you are not in the number of the dead as yet, but have come here with your intellectual faculty, having left the rest of your soul, like an anchor, in your body.

walk.label: Souls read by their colour
walk.text: The kinsman reads the stains on passing souls. A black and sordid hue is the tincture of avarice and fraud, a bloody flame-like dye betokens cruelty, and a dark violet colour like cuttlefish ink proceeds from envy.

walk.label: The place of oblivion
walk.text: He comes to a gaping chasm, fathomless downward, fringed about with the pleasing verdure of herbs and plants and a delightful prospect of flowers. It is called the place of oblivion. Souls circle it but do not enter.

walk.label: The goblet and the three daemons
walk.text: He beholds a prodigious standing goblet into which several rivers discharge themselves, one of them whiter than snow or the foam of the sea, and three daemons sitting in a triangle, blending the rivers together by certain measures.

walk.label: His guide leaves him
walk.text: He looks about for his kind and courteous guide, but the guide has quite left him, so that he sees him no more. Then he is among his own kindred and companions, who call him by name out of their punishments.

walk.label: His father out of the abyss
walk.text: He sees his father ascending out of an abyss, full of stripes, gashes and scars, who acknowledges that he had most impiously poisoned several of his guests for the sake of their gold.

walk.label: Three lakes
walk.text: Three lakes lie parallel and equidistant: one of boiling gold, one of lead exceeding cold, and the third of scaly, rugged iron. Daemons stand by them with instruments, like smiths or founders, putting souls in and drawing them out.

walk.label: Hammered into a new shape
walk.text: Souls bound for a second life are bent and hammered. Of a sudden a conspicuous light shines out, and a voice out of the light gives order for one soul to be transfigured into the shape of some more mild and gentle creature.

walk.label: Forced back as through a pipe
walk.text: A woman of admirable form takes his arm to brand him with a fiery wand; another stops her. He is hurried away with a strong and violent wind, forced as through a pipe, and wakes on the brink of his own grave.

studies.name: The Book of Arda Viraf
studies.nature: Neither a near-death account nor a spontaneous vision. Viraf is a living man chosen by lot, drugged by priests and sent deliberately to settle a dispute; Srosh greets him with 'although you have come when it is not your time', and the priests call him the messenger come from the realm of the dead to the realm of the living.
studies.type_label: Sent on purpose, and brought back
studies.finding: Chosen by lot to settle a doctrinal dispute, Viraf drinks wine and narcotic of Vishtasp from three golden cups and sleeps seven days and nights while the priests chant over him. He crosses the Chinwad bridge, is shown Hamistagan where good and sin were equal, the star, moon and sun tracks, and Garothman; then he comes back to the bridge and goes down into hell, before being carried to the eternal light.
studies.cite: The Book of Arda Viraf. Martin Haug translation, Haug and West, 1872; text at avesta.org.

walk.label: Three golden cups
walk.text: The Dasturs of the religion filled three golden cups with wine and narcotic of Vishtasp. He swallowed it, said grace while still conscious, and slept upon the clean carpet.

walk.label: Seven days away
walk.text: His soul went from the body to the Chinwad bridge of Chakat-i-Daitik, and came back on the seventh day, and went into the body.

walk.label: Srosh and Adar bow to him
walk.text: Srosh the pious and Adar the angel came to meet him, and bowed, and said: be welcome, Arda Viraf, although you have come when it is not your time.

walk.label: A pious soul's first three nights
walk.text: He watches a pious soul seated on the top of its own body for three nights, then depart into the sweet scent of trees, the air of that fragrance coming from the southern side, from the direction of God.

walk.label: Your own deeds, as a girl
walk.text: The dead man's own religion and deeds stand before him in the graceful form of a damsel, a beautiful appearance, who tells him plainly: I am your actions, O youth of good thoughts, of good words, of good deeds.

walk.label: The yellow golden balance
walk.text: At the bridge he sees Rashn the just, who held in his hand the yellow golden balance, and weighed the pious and the wicked.

walk.label: The bridge widens
walk.text: The width of that Chinwad bridge became again nine javelin-lengths. With the assistance of Srosh the pious and Adar the angel, he passed over easily, happily, courageously and triumphantly.

walk.label: Hamistagan, the ever-stationary
walk.text: They call this place Hamistagan, the ever stationary. These are the souls of those men whose good works and sin were equal. Their punishment is cold, or heat, from the revolution of the atmosphere.

walk.label: The star track
walk.text: He put forth the first footstep to the star track, and saw the souls of the pious whose radiance, ever increasing, was glittering as the stars.

walk.label: The moon track
walk.text: The second footstep was to the moon track, where he saw a great assembly of the pious, and their brightness is like the brightness of the moon.

walk.label: The sun track
walk.text: The third is the radiance they call the highest of the highest. He saw the pious on thrones and carpets made of gold: those who in the world exercised good sovereignty.

walk.label: Garothman, and the tank of water
walk.text: The fourth footstep was to the radiance of Garothman, the all-glorious. Adar showed him the blue water of a large tank, and said: this is the water which that wood exuded.

walk.label: Taken by the hand
walk.text: Vohuman the archangel arose from a throne made of gold, took hold of his hand, and brought him into the midst of Ohrmazd and the archangels. This is Ohrmazd.

walk.label: Back to the bridge
walk.text: He came back again to the Chinwad bridge, and saw the soul of one of the wicked, and the mischief and evil shown to such souls in their first three nights.

walk.label: The other woman
walk.text: A stinking cold wind comes to meet him out of the north. He saw his own religion and deeds as a profligate woman, naked, decayed, gapping, bandy-legged, lean-hipped, unlimitedly spotted. I am your bad actions.

walk.label: The greedy jaws of hell
walk.text: The greedy jaws of hell, like the most frightful pit, descending in a very narrow and fearful place, in darkness so gloomy it is necessary to hold by the hand, and in such stench that whoever inhales it will stagger and fall.

walk.label: A pit a thousand cubits deep
walk.text: Below the bridge, in a desert, hell is shown to him in the earth: as a pit, to the bottom of which a thousand cubits would not reach. And everyone in it thinks: I am alone.

walk.label: Each punishment named with its sin
walk.text: Driving snow, severe cold, the heat of brisk-burning fire, foul stench, stone and ashes, hail and rain: and for each, the deed that earned it, down to demolishing the bridge of a rapid river.

walk.label: Out, to the eternal light
walk.text: Srosh and Adar brought him forth from that dark, terrible, fearful place, and carried him to the eternal light, and the assembly of Ohrmazd and the archangels.

walk.label: A light, and nobody
walk.text: He remained astonished, for he saw a light, but he saw nobody. He also heard a voice, and he understood that this is Ohrmazd, telling him to speak truly.

walk.label: Back to the carpet
walk.text: Srosh the pious conveyed him successfully and courageously back to this carpeted place, where his body had lain seven days.

studies.name: Japan's oldest return-from-death tales
studies.nature: Listed, not walked. The tales exist and are early, but nothing in them can be quoted here yet. The honest fix is a fresh translation from the public-domain original, which this atlas has not made.
studies.finding: The Nihon Ryoiki of 822 collects Japan's earliest return-from-death stories, in which people are taken by the messengers of King Emma and sent back. The ninth-century original is out of copyright, but the only English translations, Nakamura 1973 and Watson 2013, are not, and no open text of either exists. Rather than paraphrase a translation this atlas cannot quote, the entry stays empty and says so.
studies.cite: Nihon Ryoiki, 822 CE. English translations: Nakamura K, Miraculous Stories from the Japanese Buddhist Tradition, 1973; Watson B, Record of Miraculous Events in Japan, 2013. Neither is available in open text.
studies.no_walk: No English translation of these tales is free to quote, and this atlas will not reconstruct a vision from memory. The Konjaku Monogatarishu of about 1120 retells many of the same stories and is also out of copyright; both are waiting on a translation that can be published here.

studies.name: Li E, who revived in her coffin
studies.nature: A genuine return-from-death account: she was buried half a month and revived in the coffin, and the Grand Administrator took her statement, which the text says was checked in the western district and confirmed. The narrative tells the grave-opening first; this walk follows her own order instead.
studies.finding: At the end of the Han, Li E of Wuling, a woman of sixty, died of illness and was buried outside the city. Half a month later she was summoned by the Director of Destinies in error and dismissed again, but could not get home: her family had already buried her. Her brother-in-law in the shades had the Household Bureau arrange a companion and an order to open her grave. Her neighbour split the coffin with an axe, hunting her gold, and she called out from inside it.
studies.cite: Taiping Guangji, juan 375 (the 'Returning to Life' chapters), 978 CE, citing the lost Qiongshen miyuan. The Chinese is public domain at Chinese Wikisource; no published English translation exists, so the renderings here are this site's own working translation and are labelled as such.

walk.label: Buried half a month
walk.text: At the end of the Han, Li E, a woman of Wuling aged sixty, died of illness and was buried outside the city wall. Half a month had already passed.

walk.label: Summoned by mistake
walk.text: I was summoned by the Director of Destinies by mistake. On arriving, I was dismissed.

walk.label: Her brother-in-law
walk.text: Going outside the gate she met her brother-in-law Liu Wenbo. Startled, the two of them wept facing one another.

walk.label: How am I to get back?
walk.text: I have been here more than ten days. My family have already buried me. How am I to get back by myself?

walk.label: Word to the Household Bureau
walk.text: Wenbo at once sent a gate-runner to make the matter known to the Household Bureau, the registry that held the record of her case.

walk.label: A companion, and an order
walk.text: The reply: on the western border of Wuling there is a man, Li Hei, also permitted to return, who may be her companion. And Hei is ordered to pass her neighbour's house and have Cai Zhong open the grave.

walk.label: Mind my head
walk.text: He split the coffin with an axe, hunting her gold. She suddenly called out from inside it: Cai Zhong, mind my head.

studies.name: The Apocalypse of Paul
studies.nature: Not a near-death account. Nobody is taken for dead: Paul is caught up alive, and the text deliberately refuses to settle whether his body went with him, quoting 2 Corinthians: whether in the body I know not, or whether out of the body I know not. The deaths he watches are other people's. Only a Syriac appendix has him return, and James doubts it is original.
studies.type_label: A living man shown both places
studies.finding: Caught up in the spirit to the third heaven, with the text refusing to say whether in the body or out of it. He is shown the deaths of a righteous and a sinful soul, the golden gate with its pillars of golden letters, the land of promise where the earth is seven times brighter than silver, a river of milk and honey, the city of Christ with twelve walls, then a river of fire, pits three thousand cubits deep and a well sealed with seven seals.
studies.cite: Apocalypse of Paul, 4th century. M. R. James, The Apocryphal New Testament, Oxford 1924, pp. 525-555.

walk.label: Caught up, body or not
walk.text: Whether in the body I know not, or whether out of the body I know not, God knows: such a one was caught up to the third heaven. The Syriac adds that he was caught up in the spirit and carried there.

walk.label: Angels without mercy
walk.text: Beneath the firmament he sees angels without mercy, having no pity, their countenances full of fury, their teeth sticking out of their mouths, and sparks of fire going out of their hair and their mouths.

walk.label: A good man's works stand before him
walk.text: At a righteous man's death all the works he had done for the name of God, and all his desires which he remembered and which he remembered not, stand before his face in the hour of necessity.

walk.label: The writing of the sins
walk.text: Before the judge, the angel of a sinful soul comes with a writing in his hands: these, Lord, are all the sins of this soul from its youth up until this day, even from ten years from its birth.

walk.label: The golden gate
walk.text: He is set before a gate of gold with two pillars of gold full of golden letters. These are the names of the righteous that minister to God with their whole heart, while they are yet on earth.

walk.label: Enoch, then Elias
walk.text: Inside the gate he meets Enoch, the scribe of righteousness, and then Elias. They embrace him, and weep that so few take hold of the promises.

walk.label: The land of promise
walk.text: Brought down past the firmament and out beyond the Ocean, he is told: this is the land of promise. There the earth was seven times brighter than silver.

walk.label: A river of milk and honey
walk.text: He looks round that land and sees a river flowing with milk and honey, with trees planted at the brink of it, full of fruits: every tree bearing twelve fruits in the year.

walk.label: The lake Acherusa
walk.text: He is set in a golden ship on the lake Acherusa, whose water is whiter than milk, where Michael washes the repentant before bringing them in to the city of Christ.

walk.label: The city of Christ
walk.text: The city is all of gold, with twelve walls, twelve towers and twelve gates, ringed by four rivers: honey called Phison, milk Euphrates, oil Geon and wine Tigris.

walk.label: By the way of the sunsetting
walk.text: He is taken by the way of the sunsetting. When he is come beyond the ocean he looks, and there is no light in that place, but darkness and sorrow and sadness. And he sighed.

walk.label: The river of fire
walk.text: A river of fire burning with heat, and in it a multitude of men and women sunk up to the knees, others up to the navel, others up to the lips and others up to the hair. Each depth answers a sin.

walk.label: Pits three thousand cubits deep
walk.text: He sees pits exceeding deep: the depth of that place was as it were three thousand cubits. Hardly after five hundred years do they come at the bottom.

walk.label: The well of seven seals
walk.text: He is set over a well and finds it sealed with seven seals. Opened, it stinks worse than all the torments. Inside are masses of fire burning on every side, and the mouth so strait as to take but one man in.

walk.label: The worm that sleeps not
walk.text: Further north and west is a place where there is nothing else but cold and snow, and there lies the worm that sleeps not, of the measure of one cubit, and on them were two heads.

walk.label: Michael comes down
walk.text: The heaven opens and Michael the archangel comes down out of heaven, and with him all the host of angels. For Paul's sake the damned are granted refreshment for a day and a night, for ever.

walk.label: Paradise, and the tree of life
walk.text: In Paradise he sees the head of the waters and the four rivers named by their lands, Phison, Geon, Tigris and Euphrates, and is shown the tree of life.

walk.label: Mary, with two hundred before her
walk.text: A virgin comes from afar off, with two hundred angels before her singing hymns, and salutes him by name. This is Mary the virgin, the mother of the Lord.

walk.label: Where the text stops
walk.text: The Greek, Latin and Syriac all break off inside Elijah's speech. Only a Syriac appendix adds a return: and I, Paul, returned to myself, and I knew all that I had seen. James doubts it is the original ending.
